nodes.title: Revised
nodes.body: 4-10-1994. Steve Traxler| Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution

nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name:  Ladyfish
Scientific Name: Elops saurus

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Osteichthyes
	Order:  Elopiformes
	Family:  Elopidae

Other Common Names:  bigeyed herring, jackmariddle (312), tenpounder, skipjack (327 788 858), bonefish (255), bony_fish, chiro, Francesca, John Mariggle, Liza, piojo (858).

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  No commercial fishery exists.  Smith (834) reported that the species has no food value, "the flesh being dry and bony".

Recreational:  Seldom sought by recreational fishermen but considered to be a "noted" game fish (327).  Reported as a good sport fish on light tackle (788).  Commonly caught but infrequently harvested in Everglades National Park, making up 5% of the total reported catch but less than 0.4% of the harvest (858).  Few anglers consider it a preferred species (858). Considered inedible in the United States, but eaten in limited quantities elsewhere (858).

nodes.title: Indicator
nodes.body: Ecological Role:  The young may be important forage for other fish species (858).

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Western Atlantic from Massachusetts and Bermuda through the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean to Brazil (788 858 891 1022).  Common as far north as North Carolina (788 835).  Occurs in the Indian and western Pacific Oceans (51 846).
Within Study Area:  Common throughout Florida waters.

Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body: A pelagic fish common in bays and inland waters.  Usually a schooling species throughout its range.

nodes.title: Movement/Migration
nodes.body: Reported to move on and off the mud banks in Florida Bay, possibly a feeding migration (852).

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type:  Young found along coastal beaches, in canal, bayous, lagoons, tidal ponds, creeks, rivers and mosquito impoundments (281 858).  Adults usually found in open inshore and coastal habitats (85), but may ascend rivers for considerable distances (885).

Substrate:  Found over sand and mud bottoms with no known substrate preference.

nodes.title: Temperature
nodes.body:
Eggs/Larvae:  Occur only in warm oceanic waters of 22 to 30 C (858), but larvae have been collected from 11.8 to 29.0 C (1024).  Older larvae have been collected at temperatures ranging from 18 to 30 C (858).
Juvenile/adults:  Collected at temperatures from 11.0 to 35.0 C (858).  Springer and Woodburn (664) collected them in Tampa Bay only at temperature greater than 13 C.  Susceptible to cold temperatures and reported in cold-related fish kills in Florida (236 264 836 997 1023).  Appear to be more cold tolerant than tarpon (836).

nodes.title: Salinity
nodes.body:
Eggs/larvae:  Eggs and early larvae apparently require salinities of 28.5_39.0 % for proper development (858 1024).  Older larvae have been collected at salinities ranging from 0 to 45 % (279 858).
Juvenile/adults:  Juveniles have been collected in salinities ranging from 0 to 45 % (157 279 858 1022).  Adults can tolerate a wide range of salinities (858), and although Zale and Merrifield (858) stated that they are not found in truly freshwater, in Florida they have been reported as common in all salinities in the Tampa Bay area (664), well up into freshwater rivers (835), and large individuals are found in main river channels in the Everglades (790).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode:  Sexual reproduction with external fertilization.  Oviparous.

Mating/Spawning: Spawning apparently occurs year-round and Zale and Merrifield (858) stated that it peaks in the fall.  Hoese and Moore (327) found leptocephalus larvae during most of the year, but the greatest abundance occurred in the spring and early summer.  Early larvae have been taken off North Carolina from October through May (1025).  Early larvae have been collected from March to mid-May off Galveston, Texas (19).  Larvae were found to be abundant in Florida Bay from September through December (702).

Fecundity: Fecundity and size at sexual maturity are unknown (858).

nodes.title: Eggs
nodes.body:
Larvae:  Larvae pass through several leptocephalus stages but growth rates are unknown (1024).  Length ranges for the leptocephalus stages have been given as: Stage I: 5.3 to 45.0 mm SL (1024 1027); Stage II: 18 to 45 mm SL (1024 1027); Stage III: 18 to 30 mm SL (1027). Snelson (997) collected larvae during February, April, July, August, and December indicating a prolonged spawning period or a delayed metamorphosis in the absence of suitable habitat.

Juveniles:  Minimum reported size for the juvenile stage is 35 mm SL (366).  In captivity, a growth rate of 0.626 mm/day has been reported, with larger juveniles growing an average of 0.628 mm/day (1027).  A faster growth rate of 2 mm/day was suggested under natural conditions (1027).  The following length-weight  formula for juveniles was given by Sekavec (1026):
[eq]
(Log 10) weight =  5.3295 + 3.1123(Log 10) FL
[/eq]
with weight in grams and length in millimeters.

Adults:  No information on adult growth rate is available (858).  Maximum size reported as 91 cm (840 788).  Average size about 51 cm (312).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Larvae and juveniles feed on zooplankton, but juveniles increasingly begin to feed on small fish and shrimp (279 858).  Adults are carnivorous and feed primarily on mid-water prey (310 1026).  Springer and Woodburn (664) in Tampa Bay and Snelson (997) in the Indian River Lagoon determined that the diet consisted of shrimp and fish.  Adults feed on fish which comprise about 80% of the diet and penaeid shrimp which make up about 10% of the diet (163).  Smith (834) also reported shrimp as a constituent of the diet.  Sekavec (1026) found that juvenile Gulf menhaden were about 72% of the identifiable fish found in ladyfish guts.  A diel migration onto and off of the mud banks in Florida Bay is thought to be related to feeding (852).

Juveniles:  Minimum reported size for the juvenile stage is 35 mm SL (366).  In captivity, a growth rate of 0.626 mm/day has been reported, with larger juveniles growing an average of 0.628 mm/day (1027).  A faster growth rate of 2 mm/day was suggested under natural conditions (1027).  The following length-weight  formula for juveniles was given by Sekavec (1026):
[eq]
(Log 10) weight =  5.3295 + 3.1123(Log 10) FL
[/eq]
with weight in grams and length in millimeters.

Adults:  No information on adult growth rate is available (858).  Maximum size reported as 91 cm (840 788).  Average size about 51 cm (312).

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content: Larvae and juveniles feed on zooplankton, but juveniles increasingly begin to feed on small fish and shrimp (279 858).  Adults are carnivorous and feed primarily on mid-water prey (310 1026).  Springer and Woodburn (664) in Tampa Bay and Snelson (997) in the Indian River Lagoon determined that the diet consisted of shrimp and fish.  Adults feed on fish which comprise about 80% of the diet and penaeid shrimp which make up about 10% of the diet (163).  Smith (834) also reported shrimp as a constituent of the diet.  Sekavec (1026) found that juvenile Gulf menhaden were about 72% of the identifiable fish found in ladyfish guts.  A diel migration onto and off of the mud banks in Florida Bay is thought to be related to feeding (852).
